issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder may sue on a foreign judgment where the decree was not treated as evacuee property and the Custodian did not claim rights in it.
material_facts: Both parties were evacuees under the relevant Pakistani legislation.
A final Pakistani judgment granted the decree to the claimant, who later brought a suit in India to recover on it.
The Custodian did not claim to be the decree-holder or seek to assert rights in the decree during the Pakistani proceedings.
The foreign judgment was conclusive under Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and none of that section’s exceptions applied.
issues.conclusion: The decree had not vested in the Custodian as evacuee property, and the claimant retained the right to sue on the foreign judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes a foreign judgment conclusive as to matters directly adjudicated between the parties, subject to its stated exceptions. Although Sections 2(2), 2(3), 2(5), 4 and 6 of the Pakistan Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 addressed evacuees, evacuee property and vesting in the Custodian, Section 3(1) of the Pakistan Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1957 prevented property not treated as evacuee property immediately before 1 January 1957 from being treated as such thereafter; Section 7 provided for vesting of evacuee property.

rule.if: foreign_judgment_recovery_suit and judgment_conclusive_between_parties and decree_not_treated_as_evacuee_property and custodian_never_claimed_decree

predicates.foreign_judgment_recovery_suit: The claimant brought a suit to recover on a judgment issued by a foreign court.
predicates.judgment_conclusive_between_parties: The foreign judgment directly adjudicated the matter between the same parties and was not defeated by an applicable ground for refusing conclusiveness.
predicates.decree_not_treated_as_evacuee_property: The decree was not treated as property belonging to an evacuee under the relevant property administration regime.
predicates.custodian_never_claimed_decree: The Custodian did not claim the decree or assert the decree-holder’s rights in it.

issues.definition: When a claimant sues on a conclusive foreign judgment and the decree was not treated as evacuee property nor claimed by the Custodian, the claimant retains the right to sue on that judgment.

issues.legal_issue: Time spent prosecuting in good faith an earlier proceeding that fails because the chosen forum lacks jurisdiction may be excluded when calculating limitation for a later proceeding on the same matter.
material_facts: The claimant first pursued execution of a foreign decree, although the decree could not be directly executed through that procedure and the proper remedy was a suit.
Before commencing execution, the claimant obtained advice from leading lawyers and prosecuted the proceeding diligently and in good faith.
The execution proceeding failed because it had been brought on the execution side without jurisdiction.
The later suit concerned the same underlying claim.
issues.conclusion: Section 14 of the Limitation Act applied, so the time spent prosecuting the earlier execution proceeding in good faith was excluded for limitation purposes.
issues.legal_principle: Article 117 of the Limitation Act prescribed the limitation period for a suit upon a foreign decree, and Section 14 excluded time spent prosecuting in good faith an earlier civil proceeding that could not be entertained because of a defect of jurisdiction or a similar cause. Section 14 can apply to execution proceedings where the subject matter is substantially identical, and a liberal interpretation covers circumstances that prevent a court from considering the dispute on its merits. The Court relied on its earlier decision in the Associated Hotels case, concerning the same litigation, and referred to 1959 SCR 817 at 818.

predicates.suit_on_foreign_decree: The claimant brought a suit to recover on a foreign decree.
predicates.earlier_execution_proceeding_same_subjec: The claimant had earlier pursued an execution proceeding concerning substantially the same claim.
predicates.earlier_execution_failed_for_jurisdictio: The earlier proceeding could not be entertained on its merits because of a jurisdictional defect or a similar obstacle.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_prosecuted_in_good_fa: The claimant prosecuted the earlier proceeding honestly and diligently after obtaining legal advice.

issues.definition: If a good-faith earlier proceeding on the same matter fails because of a jurisdictional or similar defect, its duration is excluded when limitation is calculated for the later suit on the foreign decree.

issues.legal_issue: A court may credit money deposited as security against a decree when the parties treated it as available to satisfy the decree but the decree-holder could not obtain it for reasons beyond the judgment-debtor’s control.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor deposited money in court as security while an appeal was pending.
After the decree was restored, the judgment-debtor asked that the deposit be applied toward the decree, and the decree-holder also claimed the deposit as intended for its benefit.
The decree-holder sought transfer of the deposit for payment toward the decree.
The deposit remained unavailable because the Pakistani Government did not carry out the court’s direction to transfer it; the judgment-debtor was not responsible for that failure.
The Court determined that the equitable adjustment arose when the judgment-debtor agreed to the adjustment and the decree-holder applied on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The deposit was to be credited toward the decree from the point at which both parties treated it as available to satisfy the decree; the remaining liability was to be calculated accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: Equity may shape a remedy where its application is consistent with positive law and established principles of conscience. A deposit made as security for a decree may be treated as belonging to the party ultimately entitled to the decree, and a judgment-debtor should not have to pay the same amount twice when the deposit cannot be applied for reasons beyond the debtor’s conduct. The Court relied on Chowthmull Manganmull v. The Calcutta Wheat and Seeds Association, Sheo Gholam Sahoo v. Rahut Hossain, Ex parte Banner, In re Keyworth, and Bird v. Barstow.

rule.if: foreign_decree_enforcement_proceeding and money_deposited_as_security_for_decree and judgment_debtor_agreed_to_application_toward_decree and decree_holder_claimed_deposit_for_decree and deposit_unavailable_for_reasons_beyond_judgment_debtor_control

predicates.foreign_decree_enforcement_proceeding: The proceeding concerned enforcement of a decree issued by a foreign court.
predicates.money_deposited_as_security_for_decree: The judgment-debtor placed money in court as security pending the outcome of proceedings concerning the decree.
predicates.judgment_debtor_agreed_to_application_to: The judgment-debtor asked that the deposited money be applied toward satisfying the decree.
predicates.decree_holder_claimed_deposit_for_decree: The decree-holder claimed the deposited money as intended to satisfy the decree.
predicates.deposit_unavailable_for_reasons_beyond_j: The decree-holder could not obtain the deposited money because of circumstances not caused or controlled by the judgment-debtor.

issues.definition: When security deposited for a foreign decree is treated by both sides as available toward the decree but cannot be obtained for reasons beyond the judgment-debtor’s control, the deposit is credited against the decree liability.

issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder alone is entitled to a court deposit made as security for a decree when both parties treated the deposit as belonging to the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor disclaimed an interest in it.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor had deposited money in court as security for a decree.
The judgment-debtor asked for the deposit to be applied toward the decree and disclaimed an interest in it.
The decree-holder claimed the deposit for itself and sought its transfer for payment toward the decree.
The deposit remained in the court’s custody despite the direction for its transfer.
issues.conclusion: The entire deposit and its accretions belonged to and could be withdrawn only by the decree-holder.
issues.legal_principle: The Court may grant equitable relief in accordance with established principles of justice and good conscience. It relied on Chowthmull Manganmull v. The Calcutta Wheat and Seeds Association, Sheo Gholam Sahoo v. Rahut Hossain, Ex parte Banner, In re Keyworth, and Bird v. Barstow for the treatment of money deposited in court as security for the party ultimately entitled to the decree.

rule.if: court_deposit_as_security_for_decree and judgment_debtor_disclaimed_interest_in_deposit and decree_holder_claimed_deposit and deposit_remained_in_court

predicates.court_deposit_as_security_for_decree: The judgment-debtor deposited money in court as security for a decree.
predicates.judgment_debtor_disclaimed_interest_in_d: The judgment-debtor stated that the deposited money should be applied to the decree and claimed no right to it.
predicates.decree_holder_claimed_deposit: The decree-holder asserted a claim to the deposited money for satisfaction of the decree.
predicates.deposit_remained_in_court: The deposited money remained held by the court rather than being paid out to the decree-holder.

issues.definition: When money deposited as security remains in court, the judgment-debtor disclaims an interest in it, and the decree-holder claims it, the decree-holder alone is entitled to withdraw it.
